We have a task: determine SMILES of unknown organic molecule given experimental data: mass spec, carbon NMR, maybe other data. We have mass spec: m/z 179.0946 (intensity 100) and isotopic pattern suggests molecular ion at 179.0946. Likely M+? The mass is 179.0946. Need to deduce formula. Use typical atomic masses: C=12.0000, H=1.007825, N=14.00307, O=15.99491. Let's compute possible formula. Use tool get_formula_from_smiles? Not yet. Could compute formula from mass. But we have carbon NMR peaks: 10 carbons (10 signals). Deltas: 166.40, 131.87, 129.70 (two), 129.01 (two), 129.00, 52.24, 43.47, 38.60. That's 10 signals, matches 10 carbons. 166.40 likely carbonyl carbon (C=O) of ester or amide. 131-129 aromatic carbons. So aromatic ring (6 carbons). 166 carbonyl (maybe amide carbonyl). 52.24 maybe O-CH3 (methoxy) or N-CH2. 43.47 maybe CH2 attached to N. 38.60 maybe CH2 attached to aromatic? Let's think.

Mass 179.0946. Let's guess formula C10H13NO2? Let's compute exact mass: C10 = 120.0000, H13 = 13*1.007825 = 13.1017, N = 14.00307, O2 = 31.9898. Sum = 179.09457. Yes matches! So formula C10H13NO2. Good. So we have 10 carbons, 13 hydrogens, 1 N, 2 O. DBE = C - H/2 + N/2 +1 = 10 - 13/2 + 1/2 +1 = 10 -6.5 +0.5 +1 =5. So DBE=5. Aromatic ring accounts for 4 DBE (one ring + three double bonds). Additional carbonyl adds 1 DBE. So consistent with aromatic ring plus carbonyl (amide or ester). So likely an aromatic amide with methoxy? Let's examine carbon NMR: carbonyl at 166.4 (amide carbonyl). Aromatic carbons around 130-129 (six). That leaves three aliphatic carbons: 52.24, 43.47, 38.60. Could be N-CH3 (52?), N-CH2 (43), CH2 attached to aromatic (38). But we have only 13 H total. Aromatic ring (C6H4?) If substituents: maybe an anilide with N-ethyl? Let's compute possibilities.

If we have an anilide: e.g., acetanilide (C8H9NO)?? Actually acetanilide formula C8H9NO? Wait acetanilide is C8H9NO? Let's check: C8H9NO? Actually acetanilide: C8H9NO? No, acetanilide is C8H9NO? Let's compute: C8H9NO? plus carbonyl O? Actually acetanilide is C8H9NO? plus O? It's C8H9NO? I'm not sure. Anyway our formula C10H13NO2 suggests maybe N-ethyl-para-methoxy? Let's think.

We have 2 oxygens: one carbonyl O, one maybe methoxy O (ester) or phenoxy? But carbonyl is amide (C=O attached to N). The other O could be part of a methoxy attached to carbonyl (i.e., methyl carbamate) or phenoxy (aryl O). But carbonyl at 166 typical for carbamate (O=C(OR)N). So maybe we have a phenyl carbamate: phenyl N-ethyl carbamate? Wait formula C10H13NO2: phenyl (C6H5) + carbonyl carbon (C=O) + O (attached to carbonyl) + N attached to ethyl (C2H5). Let's compute: phenyl C6H5, carbonyl carbon adds C1 O1, O attached to carbonyl adds O1, N adds N1, ethyl adds C2H5. Total C:6+1+2=9? Wait carbonyl carbon is already counted as part of C? yes carbonyl carbon is a carbon. So total C = 6 (ring) + 1 (carbonyl) + 2 (ethyl) =9. But we need C10. So maybe there is also a methyl attached to O (methoxy) instead of ethyl on N. Let's try phenyl carbamate with N-methyl? Actually O=C(OC)N(C)C? Let's compute: phenyl (C6H5) + carbonyl carbon (C1) + O (attached to carbonyl) + N (N) + O-methyl (CH3) + N-methyl (CH3). That's C6+1+1+1 =9? Wait O-methyl adds C1, N-methyl adds C1 => total C =6+1+1+1 =9? Actually carbonyl carbon is 1, O-methyl carbon 1, N-methyl carbon 1 => total 9. Still short.

Maybe we have phenyl attached to carbonyl via O (i.e., phenyl acetate) but we have N present. Could be anisamide (p-methoxybenzamide). Let's compute p-anisamide: C8? Actually anisamide (p-methoxybenzamide) formula C9H9NO2? Wait anisamide: C8? Let's compute: benzamide C7H7NO? Actually benzamide C7H7NO? Let's compute: benzamide C7H7NO? Actually benzamide is C7H7NO? plus O? Wait benzamide: C6H5CONH2 => C7H7NO? plus O? Actually carbonyl O is included, so formula C7H7NO? plus O? Let's compute: C6H5 (C6H5) + C=O (C1 O1) + NH2 (N1 H2) => total C7 H7? Wait H: aromatic 5 H + NH2 2 =7. So C7H7NO? plus O? Already have O from carbonyl. So formula C7H7NO? Actually O count 1. So C7H7NO? That's C7H7NO? Not matching.

Our formula C10H13NO2 suggests maybe a phenyl ring with a carbonyl attached to O (ester) and N-ethyl? Let's compute phenyl acetate (C8H8O2) plus N? Not.
